topic: Hermann Ebbinghaus (1885): 2,300 Nonsense Syllables ('WID, ZOF, KAF') & the Brutal Mathematics of Forgetting
visual_mode_reason: Hermann Ebbinghaus sitting alone with a metronome reciting 2,300 three-letter nonsense syllables ('WID, ZOF, KAF') across 7 intervals from 20 minutes to 31 days is a heroic one-man quantitative behavioral experiment staged cleanly with index cards, metronome, and logarithmic curves.

primary_case.title: Hermann Ebbinghaus's 1879-1885 Berlin one-man Nonsense-Syllable Forgetting Curve & Savings experiments (replicated by Murre & Dros, 2015)
primary_case.place: Hermann Ebbinghaus's private study, University of Berlin

people.name: Hermann Ebbinghaus
people.role: 30-year-old German philosopher-psychologist who acted as his own sole subject for years, memorizing thousands of meaningless 3-letter syllables to the tick of a 150-bpm metronome

people.name: Jaap M. J. Murre & Joeri Dros
people.role: University of Amsterdam psychologists who painstakingly replicated Ebbinghaus's entire 7-interval 1880-1885 protocol in 2015 — matching his 130-year-old curve almost point for point.

core_facts.fact: In the late 1870s, Wilhelm Wundt declared 'higher mental processes like memory can NEVER be measured experimentally.' Hermann Ebbinghaus disagreed — and spent 1879-1880 and 1883-1884 alone in Berlin testing his own memory with ruthless mathematical discipline (Über das Gedächtnis, 1885).

To strip away prior poetry or word meanings, Ebbinghaus constructed ~2,300 consonant-vowel-consonant 'nonsense syllables' (like WID, ZOF, KAF, DAX), drew random lists of 13 syllables, and read them aloud at a strict 150-strokes-per-minute metronome beat (0.4 s per syllable) at the exact same hour each day.

Instead of crude 'do you remember it yes/no?', Ebbinghaus invented the brilliant 'Savings Score' — if learning a 13-syllable list from scratch took 1,000 seconds, and relearning it tomorrow took 400 seconds, your subconscious brain 'saved' 600 seconds (60% hidden retention even when conscious recall felt like 0%).

Across 163 seven-list experiments spanning 7 retention intervals, Ebbinghaus's Savings plummeted steepest in the VERY FIRST HOUR: 58.2% saved after 20 minutes to 44.2% after 1 hour to 35.8% after 9 hours to 33.7% after 1 day to 27.8% after 2 days to 25.4% after 6 days to 21.1% after 31 days.

Look closely at 9 hours (35.8%, tested tired in the evening) vs 24 hours (33.7%, almost completely flat after a night's sleep!): Ebbinghaus noticed that overnight sleep suspiciously halted the steep drop — anticipating modern sleep-consolidation neuroscience by a century.

In 2015 (PLOS ONE), Jaap Murre and Joeri Dros put a modern 22-year-old volunteer through 70 hours of Ebbinghaus's exact 1880 nonsense-syllable torture across all 7 intervals — and reproduced Ebbinghaus's 1885 curve almost dot for dot, including the overnight 24-hour sleep plateau.
Ebbinghaus also discovered the 'Spacing Effect' in the exact same 1885 book: 38 repetitions spread across 3 days beat 68 massed cramming repetitions in a single sitting.

And when Ebbinghaus memorized meaningful verses of Lord Byron's Don Juan instead of nonsense syllables, he needed only ONE-TENTH as many repetitions — proving meaning acts like Velcro against the forgetting cliff.
In Ebbinghaus's (1885) relearning-savings tables, retention fell steeply from roughly 58% (58.2%) at 20 minutes to 44% (44.2%) at 1 hour, 33.7% at 1 day, and 21% (21.1%) at 31 days.

wow_facts.fact: More than HALF of raw unreviewed information (41.8% lost in 20 minutes; 55.8% lost in 1 hour!) falls off the cliff before lunch — then the remaining ~25% clings stubbornly for a whole month.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Forgetting isn't a slow linear leak; it is a vertical first-hour waterfall followed by a long tail.

wow_facts.fact: Even when you swear 'I forgot 100% of my college Spanish,' Ebbinghaus's Savings Score proves those traces are hiding underneath — relearning takes a fraction of the original time.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Zero conscious recall does NOT mean zero memory left in the brain.

wow_facts.fact: 130 years later (Murre & Dros 2015), a modern student repeated Ebbinghaus's brutal 70-hour syllable marathon and landed almost directly on top of Ebbinghaus's 1885 ink dots — right down to the overnight sleep bump.
wow_facts.why_surprising: One obsessively controlled human subject discovered a universal law of human memory.

wow_facts.fact: 38 spaced reviews across three days crushed 68 last-night cramming repetitions in Ebbinghaus's own 1885 ledger — every modern flashcard app (Anki, SuperMemo, Duolingo) runs on his 1885 math.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Spaced repetition was born in 1885 on paper cards and a ticking metronome.

misconceptions.myth: You lose 80% of a meaningful lecture or book story within 24 hours just like WID-ZOF-KAF.
misconceptions.truth: The steep 56%-in-one-hour cliff applies to MEANINGLESS rote facts; Ebbinghaus himself showed meaningful connected text (Byron's poetry) takes 10x fewer repetitions and decays dramatically slower.

misconceptions.myth: If you draw a blank on a test question, your study session was completely erased.
misconceptions.truth: Ebbinghaus's Savings method proves sub-threshold traces remain intact and spring back rapidly on a brief review.

misconceptions.myth: Reading notes ten times in a row on Sunday night locks them into long-term memory.
misconceptions.truth: Massed cramming inflates short-term fluency for 20 minutes before plunging down the 9-hour cliff; spacing reviews right before the curve bends flattens decay.

everyday_hooks: Walking out of a 1-hour conference talk feeling inspired, then realizing at dinner you can barely name two bullet points.
Re-picking up piano chords or high-school French years later and marveling how much faster it comes back ('Savings').
Using 10 minutes of spaced flashcards (Day 1, Day 3, Day 7) to beat 3 hours of panicked midnight cramming.
